decisions.quote: If statistical significance is taken as a criterion for successful replication, we failed to replicate the two key effects in the LK studies: the main effect of Dative in Experiment 1 (critical region), and the interaction of Dative and Adjunct in Experiment 2 (post-critical region). If a frequentist p-value were to be computed for these effects, none would come out even close to significant in any of the four attempts.
decisions.reason: Across seven direct replication experiments of Levy & Keller (2013), the authors explicitly state that their case study demonstrates that the original statistically significant results overestimate the true effect and are non-replicable (p. 6), that Experiments 1-4 failed to replicate the two key effects of LK's Experiments 1 and 2 on total reading times as well as all other originally significant dependent measures (p. 27 and fn. 9), and that the high-precision 100-participant Experiment 7 (designed to reach their target ROPE precision of <= 40 ms credible interval width) likewise provided no grounds for claiming the Load-Distance interaction and yielded results consistent with no effect (pp. 40-41). Per the codebook, 'uninformative' is not used merely because estimates are imprecise, nonsignificant, or accompanied by philosophical caution against affirming the null hypothesis, especially when the paper also includes a high-precision replication (Experiment 7) that disconfirms the focal interaction claim. Thus the shipped outcome 'failed' is correct.

decisions.quote: In the number agreement experiments, study 1 is the ungrammatical agreement data from Experiment 1 of Dillon et al. (2013); studies 2-5 are the experiments reported in Lago et al. (2015), and 6-10 are from Wagers et al. (2009). Studies 11 and 12 are from Cunnings and Sturt (2018). The estimates shown in the figure were computed by fitting a linear mixed model (with full covariance matrices for random effects) in Stan using log-transformed reading times, and then by back-transforming the estimate of the facilitation effect to milliseconds. Our estimates may be slightly different from the original published estimates in some cases because we did not remove any data.
decisions.reason: Wrong original / insufficient evidence from source: Dillon et al. (2013) is one of 12 datasets (10 from the prior meta-analysis of Jäger et al., 2017) plotted in the General Discussion and Appendix C merely as an incidental background illustration that wide credible intervals are common in psycholinguistics, rather than a central target the paper set out to test. Moreover, even in the blind coding, computational reproducibility was 'not checked' and substantive robustness for this specific study is 'cannot_be_determined' (the text reports only pooled summary ranges and an unattributed count across the 10 studies). Under the audit rules, incidental re-estimations with 'not checked' and 'cannot_be_determined' outcomes establish no omitted-target error.
